groups.label: Education in Music and Gymnastic
groups.summary: Socrates establishes that musical and physical training directly shape the soul, balancing spiritedness with harmony and instilling an affinity for virtue. Preserving these strict cultural forms without innovation serves as the foundation for civic order and moral stability.
groups.rationale: These four nodes cover the Books III and IV discussions of early education, emphasizing how rhythm, harmony, and gymnastic discipline cultivate virtue in the soul and protect the state.

groups.label: Psychology and Non-Contradiction
groups.summary: Socrates introduces the principle of non-contradiction, establishing that the same entity cannot act in opposite ways at the same time in the same part. Applying this rule reveals that the soul contains three distinct components: the rational, spirited, and appetitive.
groups.rationale: These adjacent Book IV nodes present the logical formulation of non-contradiction and its immediate application to demonstrate the tripartite division of the soul.

groups.label: Civic Cohesion and Nature
groups.summary: Socrates clarifies that natural differences relevant to civic duties determine societal roles rather than incidental physical distinctions. He argues that unity constitutes the ultimate civic good, comparing an ideal state to an organic body where all citizens feel shared joy and sorrow.
groups.rationale: These Book V nodes focus on political organization, social roles according to relevant nature, and the supreme importance of common feeling and state cohesion.

groups.label: Philosophers and Eternal Forms
groups.summary: Ideal patterns serve as evaluative standards regardless of complete empirical realization, pursued by philosophers who desire all of wisdom. While sensory lovers confuse manifold particulars with real forms like absolute beauty, true philosophers apprehend the singular, unified reality of the Forms.
groups.rationale: These nodes bridge the role of political ideals with the definition of the philosopher, contrasting the apprehension of singular Forms against absorption in sensory copies.

groups.label: Epistemology: Knowledge vs Opinion
groups.summary: Faculties are distinguished by their functional domains and outcomes, demonstrating that infallible knowledge and fallible opinion govern different spheres. Opinion occupies an intermediate position between being and not-being, corresponding to fluctuating sensory particulars, thereby dividing lovers of opinion from lovers of true wisdom.
groups.rationale: This sequence from Book V develops the technical epistemology distinguishing faculties, the ontological status of sensory particulars, and the division between opinion and philosophical knowledge.
